name: Tortoise
lede: Tortoise is the dark mottled brown of tortoiseshell, shown here as one flat reddish brown, which Maerz and Paul recorded as first used in 1730.

sections.title: The shell and the word
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary has the rare adjective *testudinarious*, meaning having the color and other characteristics of a tortoise or tortoise-shell [1]. Our swatch is a single reddish brown from Maerz and Paul, who record the name as first used in 1730, but the shell it names is mottled, so no one flat color can stand for it [2].

The books say little more about the color itself. What they do offer is a few stories where a tortoise appears. Balfour-Paul reports that some woven indigo patterns in West Africa carry names such as "land tortoise" [3].

sections.title: A gilded tortoise
sections.body: In Huysmans' novel *À rebours*, as Batchelor tells it, the hero Des Esseintes wants a moving, dark object to set off the gleaming tints of a carpet, so he has a live tortoise gilded and set with gems [4]. The animal is dead the next day [4]. Batchelor reads it as a moral tale about cosmetics that decorate and suffocate [4]. It is a story about the color of its shell being covered over, not about the shell's own brown.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This brown is common in paintings: it appears in 2,609 of 23,781 paintings, more often than 92 per cent of named colors [5]. It is most often an accent within the painting, in 40 per cent of the 1,195 paintings where it is measurable [5]. George Catlin carries it in 13 of his 50 paintings here, 4.4 times the baseline of the museums his work comes from [5]. Its nearest named neighbors are [[brown]] and [[bay]] [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test. [5]
